video_title: The New Market Structure: AI Concentration and the Largest Hedge Fund Degrossing in 10 Years
gist: Weekly market wrap arguing October's tech selloff was the largest hedge fund degrossing on record rather than a bear market, with index breadth strong, AI financing concentration driving hyperscaler CDS, and Anthropic's S-1, memory/optical demand and Eli Lilly as supports. Visser says the new regime is 'strikeout, strikeout, home run' so exiting on bubble fears is costly.

themes.theme: October deleveraging, not a bear market

insights.claim: The S&P 500 fell only 93bp in October and 60bp in the final week, with 9 of 11 sectors up for the month and 327 of 500 names up, so the scary headlines overstate the damage; Visser calls it a rotation and hedge fund deleveraging.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Index-level damage is small; the pain is concentrated in crowded AI/hedge fund positions.
insights.quote: If you're looking at the market, this has been a rotation.

insights.claim: Share of S&P 500 names above their 50-day moving average went from 20% at the start of October to 61% at the end, confirming broad rotation under the index surface.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Breadth recovered even as headline tech sold off; supports a rotation, not a top, read.

insights.claim: Morgan Stanley prime brokerage data shows October was the largest hedge fund degrossing it has recorded, larger than the July 'situational awareness' episode, and it has spread beyond equities into credit (CoreWeave) and other areas.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Forced selling rather than fundamentals drove AI weakness; ending a degrossing is hard to time.

insights.claim: Visser compares the episode most closely to the GameStop hedge fund unwind in 2021, a deleveraging inside a good economy, since other 6%+ S&P drawdowns became 15%+ declines tied to recession or tightening; the S&P was about 4% off its high.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Positioning-driven unwinds in strong economies tend to resolve without a bear market, unlike macro-driven ones.

insights.claim: Charlie McElligott's pair-trade monitor showed 124 pair trades unwinding with 47 moving more than three sigma, a 'traumatic risk management unwind' concentrated in AI winners with high Sharpe ratios.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Crowded long/short AI books were the transmission mechanism.

insights.claim: Visser expects no re-leveraging soon, so dry powder exists but hedge funds may stay jumpy until the VIX falls back to around 16 and the S&P regains its 50-day average; he sees head-and-shoulders/island-top charts that explain bearishness but a monthly chart that looks fine.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Near-term chop likely; the monthly structure does not signal a top.

insights.claim: The VIX barely moved (only briefly above 20) and IG CDX stayed far below March levels, so credit and vol markets showed little panic versus equities.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Systemic stress is absent; the stress is idiosyncratic to AI financing names.

insights.claim: The Goldman Sachs AI winners-versus-losers pair basket gave back essentially the whole year's gain, and the Goldman VIP hedge fund index relative to the S&P is the positioning chart behind the AI unwind.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: AI trade has already de-risked heavily; downside from here requires a true bubble.

themes.theme: Market structure: strikeout, strikeout, home run

insights.claim: Visser argues market structure has permanently changed so investors must accept 'strikeout, strikeout, strikeout, home run': Nvidia returned about 30% annualized over 30 months, and four months, under 15% of the period, delivered the entire move and more.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Exiting on bubble fears or broken charts risks missing the few outsized months.
insights.quote: you have to get used to strikeout, strikeout, strikeout, home run.

insights.claim: The S&P's recent return was concentrated: about 150% of the return since September 13 months ago came in a short window when oil was feared at 200 and the Strait of Hormuz was shut, reflecting that nobody wanted to buy at the lows.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Fear-driven lows deliver the returns; market timing out of fear is costly.

insights.claim: Visser says he flagged in March that the market was leaving the QE-era 'SaaS world' of no-debt, always-beating tech for a world of rising oil, rates, credit spreads and volatility, which resembles emerging-market conditions he lived through.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Regime of higher rates and volatility is structural; past playbooks fail.
insights.quote: This environment is what I lived in in emerging markets.

insights.claim: Visser holds that rates stay high unless inflation and labor fall sharply (eventually from AI), so he rejects any return to the zero-rate era anytime soon.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Assume higher cost of capital for AI buildout.

insights.claim: Google fell 12% relative to the S&P in a week, the biggest relative drop since the financial crisis, and 2025 included record one-day wipeouts: Meta about $250 billion, Google $500 billion, Microsoft $357 billion, Nvidia $589 billion on DeepSeek (about 20% of Russell 2000 market cap).
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Mega-cap weights are so large that single-name moves move the index and portfolios.

insights.claim: The four hyperscalers (Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Meta) are unchanged relative to the S&P since 2020 and have gone nowhere since October of last year, yet carry violent swings because they moved from no debt to heavy borrowing.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Treat their drop as multiple compression from capex funding, not a business collapse.
insights.quote: They have the most pristine balance sheets despite the fact that their CDS is widening out.

insights.claim: Hyperscalers and the AI hardware/memory trade have become correlated: earlier hyperscalers lagged while semis worked because funds were underweight semis, but now doubts about hyperscaler capex hit memory and semis together.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: AI supply chain now trades as one factor tied to capex confidence.

insights.claim: Visser advises RIAs and advisors to reduce hyperscaler weights in ETFs and portfolios, increase exposure to the agentic compute side, and hold longevity (Eli Lilly) and energy.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Portfolio-construction recommendation: diversify away from mega-cap concentration.

insights.claim: Apple trades at about a 40 P/E while other hyperscalers are hit because investors pay for quality balance sheet and Apple has not spent money; the Bloomberg quality index rotation has run since July when credit fears began.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Quality bid persists while 10-year yields stay above 4.5%.

themes.theme: AI financing, credit and Treasury supply

insights.claim: AI-related debt and equity/SPV issuance has exceeded $1 trillion this year, concentrated in about 16 companies, and the binding constraint is investor absorption and concentration limits rather than demand, with insurers' demand for long-duration debt falling roughly 50% because of exposure limits.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Financing shifts to private markets and SPVs; CDS widening reflects supply concentration, not bubble proof.

insights.claim: A Goldman Sachs credit discussion expects AI financing needs to peak in 2027, with hyperscaler capex at 27% then 33% then 35% of IG market growth, and sees monetization delays determining borrowing needs; Visser says hyperscalers can still lever up significantly.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Peak external financing around 2027 could strengthen credit afterwards.

insights.claim: Gavin Baker suggested the AI buildout may be approaching peak external financing, because cloud contracts reprice higher at renewal and accelerate cloud revenue and operating cash flow.
insights.speaker: Gavin Baker (as cited by Visser)
insights.so_what: Credit spreads on AI names could stabilize once cash flow replaces external funding.

insights.claim: Oracle said it would raise no more than $20 billion of additional financing through 2030 and become free cash flow positive in the second half of 2028, reaching $30 billion in 2029; its CDS had its best week since September of last year and the biggest tightening in its history.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: First AI-credit bellwether to signal lower capital needs; market rewarded it.

insights.claim: Microsoft's CDS has not widened because it had borrowed nothing, and its new $25 billion borrowing shows the CDS moves reflect concentration of supply rather than a bubble.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Watch issuers' supply, not just fundamentals, for CDS direction.

insights.claim: Triple-C spreads are wider than in 2022 and yields around 16%, which Visser takes to mean many bankruptcies are coming as yields are unlikely to fall much; mortgage rates are up about 100bp since April and a further 60bp since Jackson Hole.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Stress is in the weak-credit tail and housing affordability while IG remains calm.

insights.claim: Visser flags the November 4 quarterly refunding as a missed risk: Treasury Secretary Bessent could cut long bond sales or cancel 20- and 30-year auctions in favor of bills, a version of yield curve control, given affordability politics before the midterms.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A cut in long-end supply would lower term yields and help Bitcoin, silver and duration-sensitive assets.
insights.quote: Bessam will likely cut US long bond sales next month

insights.claim: The 10-year yield peaked around October 7 and closed below its 50-day average for the first time, with Visser seeing a possible move toward 4.5%, though real yields were high because hyperscaler debt dominated the long end.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Lower yields remove a bear trade; CTAs are vulnerable.

insights.claim: Market-implied odds of a Fed hike stayed near 75% after Warsh's hawkish remarks, but Visser doubts a December hike is guaranteed if stocks rally and credit improves; TLT is basically unchanged since Warsh's speech.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Hike pricing may be too aggressive; long-end tightening already does the work.

insights.claim: Goldman estimates show software, energy and tariff effects rolling off inflation this year, and year-over-year DRAM price growth is collapsing, so the memory-phone component of PCE will also fade.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Disinflationary comps support lower yields into next year.

insights.claim: Anthropic's S-1 revealed about $132 billion of cash, a surprise to the street, with revenue growing far faster than expenses and half the Fortune 500 already customers; Visser sees this as removing IPO risk and reducing financing fears.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Large cash balance secures capex commitments and reduces credit-market overhang.
insights.quote: This was a very big surprise to the street

insights.claim: Visser put the S-1 into ChatGPT, which produced a base case of roughly $100 billion (95 to 110) for a scenario he cites, and he argues the S-1 shows enterprise adoption is still very early.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: LLM-derived scenario, treat as exploratory.

insights.claim: Visser says he would not want to own Anthropic long term because model business faces commoditization, noting he personally uses ChatGPT, Grok and Gemini more than Claude, though he considers the IPO a near-term positive.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Valuation durability in model makers is uncertain even if the IPO goes well.

insights.claim: GPU rental prices are rising and compute has moved into contango, meaning future capacity is more expensive; Baker argues public investors focus on 2027 capacity online while pricing shows tightness.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Compute scarcity contradicts the glut/bubble thesis.

insights.claim: S&P 500 earnings growth is around 25-30% in the quarter, guidance is stronger than last quarter, revenue beats exceed September expectations, and European earnings growth rivals the US for the first time in years.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Fundamentals remain strong; breadth of earnings is widening beyond the Mag 7.

insights.claim: Capex is broadening beyond hyperscalers to enterprises, sovereigns and on-prem buyers (Jensen Huang's $90 trillion framing), which means more capital demand, multiple compression and higher-for-longer rates but a widening beneficiary set.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Beneficiaries include suppliers and financial firms, not just hyperscalers.

insights.claim: Memory demand shows no slowdown: SK Hynix and Micron are signing contracts to 2030, and Elon Musk argues robots will be the largest consumers of RAM; Visser raised his Micron position and expects embodied agents to start next year.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Memory is a multi-year supply-constrained trade tied to humanoids.

insights.claim: Corning reported accelerating demand pressing against capacity, with optical connectivity per GPU potentially expanding tenfold and conviction that it accelerates in 2028, mainly a Vera Rubin and Feynman story; Visser bought optical names after the bounce.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Optical is supply-constrained with a step-up in per-GPU content.

insights.claim: Visser is wary of Marvell's rumored Lumentum acquisition because it removes the possibility of a quick doubling, and would reduce Marvell on a bounce if the deal happens, while diversifying into other optical names.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Acquirer risk dampens upside in a favored AI name.

insights.claim: Visser's screen of weekly technicals (advance/pullback stage, MACD histogram turning up, rising 200-day) found only five qualifying AI names, and the average RSI of his 100-name index hit its lowest level of the year, suggesting a near low.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Technically oversold AI basket; SMH held its 200-day average.

insights.claim: Microsoft offered to buy out about 60,000 employees, 27% of headcount, which Visser reads as stage one of AI productivity with revenue per employee soaring and labor versus capital becoming an issue next year; he says GDP cannot measure AI productivity.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Margin expansion and labor displacement are the AI productivity tells, not GDP.

insights.claim: Visser expects Eli Lilly to be the largest S&P 500 stock by the end of 2030; it reported 39% year-over-year revenue growth to $24.4 billion, with US GLP-1 penetration around 10% of 110 million overweight people and international only about 2%.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Falling GLP-1 prices expanding volume is a Jevons paradox; long runway.
insights.quote: I think this will be the biggest stock before we get to 20 the end of 2030

insights.claim: Bitcoin fell 4% on the week despite the largest hack in history at Binance and was down 7% in October, becoming correlated with SMH; Visser's favorite trade is long Bitcoin versus short the Nasdaq-100 and his Elliott Wave count sees a 38% retracement in wave four before a major move.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Crypto trades as a tech-risk proxy now; relative-value expression preferred.

insights.claim: Visser gave ChatGPT materials from IonQ, Google, IBM and others and it estimated about a 15% chance IonQ delivers cryptographically relevant quantum by December 2028, so he discounts the quantum-breaks-Bitcoin fear.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Quantum threat to crypto is overdone near-term.

insights.claim: Visser rotated into silver and crypto from AI and still likes silver because central banks and tech companies are buying and CTAs are heavily short, but calls its chart poor and was hurt this week.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Silver is a crowded-short contrarian setup, not a confident bet.

insights.claim: Tokenization is advancing: Google is developing a Bitcoin and crypto custody service for institutions, Solana RWA hit an all-time high, and the DTCC tokenization service went live; names highlighted include Ondo, Centrifuge, Figure and Providence.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Institutional rails for tokenized assets are arriving.
